facts.claim: P3 asks students to investigate Singapore’s environment and responses to its challenges.
facts.note: The inquiry question is verbatim in the linked evidence record.

facts.claim: P3 knowledge outcomes cover recognising and mapping places; explaining environmental effects of actions; describing protection, challenges and adaptation to needs.
facts.note: Paraphrase. The complete list is in the linked PDF, Knowledge Outcomes column.

facts.claim: P3 skills cover information gathering, guided observation and evaluation, scaffolded decisions, group communication, collaboration and presentation.
P3 values cover resource responsibility, recognising beliefs, considering ethical consequences, curiosity, community and environmental care, belonging, and responsible information use.
P3 content includes consequences for the environment, cleanliness and greenery, conservation, and responsible resource use at home, school and in the community.
P3 explicitly connects changing land use with meeting needs.
Food content addresses farming constraints in Singapore, changing kinds of farms, and advances in farming technology.
Housing content addresses provision challenges, changing living conditions, and improvements to public housing estates as society’s needs change.
Transport content addresses provision challenges and change in Singapore’s transport system.
The existing Atlas coast file contains L0–L5 dated land geometries and a separate present-day coast line; L5 starts on 1961-01-01 and has no end date.
facts.note: An open-ended implementation interval is not evidence that the coast stayed unchanged after 1961. New post-1961 coast frames need dated real map evidence.

facts.claim: URA Master Plans map permissible land use and density; differences between editions are zoning changes, not direct measurements of observed use.

SFA describes soil-grown land farms in Lim Chu Kang and Sungei Tengah; indoor farms can stack crops, use artificial light and recirculate nutrient water; rooftops can support soil beds or hydroponics.
facts.note: These are current farm types, not historical parcel boundaries. Technology does not by itself establish a measured yield or energy saving.

facts.claim: SFA dates Singapore’s first indoor farm to 2014.
JTC dates the conception of Jurong Industrial Estate to 1961.
JTC describes Jurong Island as a project joining seven southern islands into one 3,000-hectare landmass for the energy and chemicals industry.
facts.note: The release reports the island as a whole; it does not provide decade-by-decade reclamation polygons.

facts.claim: NParks records a nationwide tree-planting campaign in 1963, creation of the Parks and Trees Unit in 1967, and the Garden City Action Committee in 1970.
facts.note: These institutional milestones cannot be used as dates for all mapped park polygons. Current park boundaries are a separate dataset.

facts.claim: A joint 25 May 2026 release describes proposed agriculture to the north of Lim Chu Kang and future defence uses in the south; its annex maps affected farm plots and indicative areas.
facts.note: Indicative future plan, not evidence of a completed land-use change or an open geospatial licence.

facts.claim: A September 1986 government release proposed 2,000 hectares of agrotechnology parks for 1986–1992, mainly in the northwest including Lim Chu Kang/Neo Tiew. Its first tender covered 120 hectares at Sungei Tengah, Murai and Loyang.
facts.note: A programme target, not a measurement of land already developed. The NAS accession stamp says 29 September 1986; release code encodes 3 September 1986. Read scanned original visually.

facts.claim: Kampong Wak Sumang received piped water, electricity, paved roads and drainage during the 1960s.
facts.note: A named counterexample to any claim that every kampong lacked services throughout the 1960s. Do not generalise one settlement’s experience to all.

facts.claim: FAO reports 937 hectares used for farming in 2000 within agrotechnology parks covering about 1,465 hectares, citing AVA’s 2004 statistics.
facts.note: Secondary quotation of AVA2004 statistics; original AVA page not recovered. Area of estate infrastructure differs from cultivated/occupied farming area.

facts.claim: The Bukit Ho Swee fire occurred on 25 May 1961.
The fire burned about 100 acres (0.4 square kilometres), including homes and workplaces.
About 16,000 people lost their homes and four people died.
The cause of the fire remains unknown; do not assign a cause in the textbook.
NLB records that all remaining affected families had been rehoused by February 1962.
After acquisition of the fire site and adjacent land, HDB built 12,562 flats in the area by 1967, including one-room emergency flats.
Around 1960, some families occupied small shophouse cubicles in buildings shared with other households.
Thousands lived in informal settlements lacking household piped water, reliable electricity and adequate sanitation/waste disposal. Do not generalise this to every kampong.
HDB responded to the housing shortage with high-rise construction, communal corridors and standardised layouts.
NHB records five HDB blocks completed in nine months to house families displaced by the Bukit Ho Swee fire.
Housing estates incorporated neighbourhood amenities, including schools, clinics and libraries, alongside homes.
For some residents, moving from kampong houses or shophouses to high-rise flats initially involved difficult adjustments.
NHB describes traditional kampong houses with sloping roofs, often thatched with palm fronds, and raised floors that help ventilation and coping with wet ground.
Au Seck Ngee’s family described leaving their familiar kampong for their first flat as a major life change. They needed HDB help explaining English contracts.
facts.evidence_type: Named family testimony, not a statement about every resident

facts.claim: The Singapore Mandarin Database describes kampong neighbours as interacting frequently and caring for one another.
SIT planned Queenstown as Singapore’s first satellite town in 1953. This is a planning milestone, not a whole-town completion year.
Toa Payoh land preparation took place in 1964, ahead of HDB’s second five-year building programme in 1965; HDB calls it its first comprehensively planned town.
Ang Mo Kio’s first slab blocks were built in 1973, within Neighbourhoods 2 and 3.
Construction of Tampines New Town began in 1979.
The first Tengah residents collected keys at Plantation Acres and Plantation Grange in August 2023.
All residential blocks at Tengah’s first two BTO projects, Plantation Acres and Plantation Grange, were completed in December 2023.
Upper Peirce Reservoir was completed in 1975 and officially opened on 27 February 1977.
NHB dates formation of Pandan Reservoir by enclosing the estuary swamps with an earthen dyke to 1974. This differs from completion of the water scheme in 1975.
A 1979 ministerial speech identifies the Kranji–Pandan Water Scheme as completed in 1975. Use scheme completion rather than imposing a single reservoir construction year.
Bedok Reservoir was completed in 1986; its site had previously been a sand quarry. Reservoir conversion works began in 1983.
PUB’s trail chronology dates the dam across the Seletar River mouth to 1986. The resulting Sungei Seletar Reservoir was renamed Lower Seletar Reservoir in 1992.
Marina Barrage opened in 2008.
Marina Reservoir was commissioned in 2010, distinct from the barrage’s opening in 2008.
Punggol and Serangoon reservoirs were commissioned in 2011.

gaps.detail: The current official MOE syllabus page links a PDF whose cover says January2024. The named July2024 URL is indexed but returned404 in direct download and a bot challenge in web access. July-specific wording and differences remain unverified.

Full verbatim outcome lists are not reproduced because quotations from one copyrighted source are limited. The inquiry question and two short syllabus extracts are verbatim; remaining outcomes/content are explicitly paraphrased with exact printed-page and PDF-page locators. The downloaded official PDF is retained in sources/moe-jan2024.pdf.
No complete licence-cleared observed land-use polygon series for1950s–1980s was verified. Master Plans are planning snapshots; archive access and academic publication do not establish open rights.

Published maps support selected dates/areas, not a complete verified decade-by-decade reclamation dataset. Glaser1991 full map pages were not accessible. Wong1992 is identified via Hesp1995; original chapter not inspected.
No open whole-island1960s kampong-farm boundary dataset was verified. The1986 government annexes locate agricultural land and proposed estate uses; their map reuse licence remains unverified.

Historical farm area figures use rounded decades and different definitions. The2000 FAO value cites unrecovered AVA2004 statistics. Current food-farm licence counts exclude some non-food farming; no fully harmonised annual farm-area series was verified.

Reservoir milestones here are selected verified examples, not a complete17-reservoir commissioning register. Western reservoir dates and earlier extension footprints need further primary-source checks. Current polygons must not be back-projected unchanged.

First services and selected opening stages are verified; a complete station-to-station opening register including every extension to2026 is not assembled. A first line-opening date cannot activate all later segments.
A whole new town does not have one defensible completion year. Use documented planning, first blocks, keys and project-completion events; current HDB stock also omits demolished buildings.
